content: Oily fish, also known as oil-rich or pelagic fish, are characterized by the presence of oils distributed throughout their fillets and in the belly cavity surrounding the gut, unlike white fish, where oil is primarily concentrated in the liver. The oil content in oily fish fillets can reach up to 30%, though this percentage varies depending on the species and individual fish. These fish typically inhabit the pelagic zones of the ocean. Oily fish are an excellent dietary source of vitamins A and D, as well as omega-3 fatty acids. Due to these nutritional properties, oily fish are considered more beneficial for human health compared to white fish. Omega-3 fatty acids in oily fish have been associated with potential health benefits, including alleviation of depressive symptoms, reduction in the risk of cardiovascular diseases, and improvement in inflammatory conditions such as arthritis. Dementia A French study published in 2002 in the British Medical Journal followed 1,674 elderly individuals residing in southern France over a seven-year period. The study examined the relationship between their consumption of meat versus seafood and the development of dementia symptoms. The findings indicated that individuals who consumed fish at least once per week had a significantly lower risk of being diagnosed with dementia during the study period. However, the study could not definitively determine whether fish consumption directly protected against dementia or whether individuals with dementia were less likely to consume fish. Additionally, participants with higher levels of education were found to have both a lower risk of dementia and higher fish consumption, though the interplay between these factors remains unclear. Cardiovascular Health Consuming oily fish twice per week has been associated with a reduced risk of sudden cardiac death caused by myocardial infarction, primarily through the prevention of cardiac arrhythmias. Eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA), a key component of fish oils, is metabolized in the body into resolvins, which exhibit potent anti-inflammatory properties. These anti-inflammatory effects are beneficial for cardiovascular health and may also help alleviate symptoms of arthritis. Recommended Consumption In 1994, the UK Committee on Medical Aspects of Food and Nutrition Policy (COMA) recommended consuming at least two portions of fish per week, with one portion being oily fish.1 micrograms per kilogram of body weight per day, with a corresponding blood mercury limit of 5.8 micrograms per liter. The UK guidelines suggest that men, boys, and women beyond childbearing age can safely consume up to four portions of oily fish per week (one portion equals 140 grams or approximately 4.9 ounces). Women of childbearing age, including those who are pregnant or breastfeeding, as well as girls, are advised to limit their intake to two portions per week. There are no restrictions on the consumption of white fish. In the United States, the EPA and USDA guidelines (as of 2007) recommend limiting the consumption of fatty fish with high methylmercury levels, such as tilefish, king mackerel, shark, and swordfish. Pregnant and nursing women, as well as children under six years of age, are advised to avoid these high-MeHg fish entirely. For moderate and low-MeHg fish, this population should limit their intake to 12 ounces or less per week, with albacore tuna restricted to 6 ounces or less per week. Plant-Based Omega-3 Sources Concerns regarding contamination, dietary preferences, or limited fish supply have prompted research into plant-based sources of omega-3 fatty acids, such as flaxseed and hempseed oil. Studies have shown that lactating women who supplemented their diets with flaxseed oil experienced increased levels of alpha-linolenic acid (ALA) and eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) in their blood and breast milk. However, no significant changes were observed in the levels of docosahexaenoic acid (DHA).
